introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. English Language 2 (0730), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Paper 2: Section A - Summary and Text Reconstruction; Section B - Composition; Section C - Prescribed Texts. Duration: three hours.**

Answer BOTH questions in SECTION A and ONE EACH from SECTIONS B and C in the SAME Answer Booklet, beginning each section on a new page.

Read all instructions on BOTH the question paper and the answer booklet very carefully. Failure to obey these instructions or to number your work as on the question paper will cause you to lose marks.

Any unusual mark, sign or unnecessary disclosure of your identity will be considered as an attempt to cheat and will earn you a penalty.

In the SUMMARY question, use mainly your own words. Indiscriminate copying of portions of the passage as your answer will be penalised.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

A pre-prepared or memorised composition will be severely sanctioned.
enonce_intro_markdown:
**SECTION B - COMPOSITION (20 marks)**

Mark distribution: Content and Organisation (06 marks); Expression (08 marks); Accuracy (06 marks).

Choose ONE topic to write about from the list below. You are advised to write clearly and effectively, to spell and punctuate correctly, and to ensure that your writing is appropriate in style and content to the topic chosen. Avoid obscene language and do not disclose your identity. You should write between 500 and 550 words.

questions.corrige_markdown:
**Plan**

1. State which picture is used (Picture A) and describe what it shows.
2. Link it to a story: Pa Nkwain, a gold digger in the East Region.
3. Develop the day: the work, the dialogue, the danger, the small discovery.
4. Close with the meaning of the picture: courage, patience, dignity of manual work.

**Model composition (514 words)**

I have chosen Picture A, which shows a man in a battered hat crouching on rough ground, working the earth with his bare hands beside some shallow pans. To me, the scene speaks of the hard labour of a small-scale miner, and it reminded me of Pa Nkwain, a gold digger whom I met in a village in the East Region.

Pa Nkwain's day began long before dawn. Wearing the same hat that had protected him from the sun for twenty years, he walked two kilometres to the stream with a shovel, a bucket and his metal pans. There was no machine, no helmet, no boots. Whatever the earth gave him, he would earn with his own hands and the sweat of his brow. When I joined him one morning, the ground was already wet and heavy with mud, and he was kneeling in it, scooping gravel into a pan, swirling it with water and peering at the heavy sand that settled at the bottom.

"Look carefully, my son," he said without lifting his head. "Gold does not shout. It only shines for those who are patient." I watched him repeat the same movement a hundred times. His fingers were cracked, his back was bent like a bow, and the sun, climbing higher, burnt the back of his neck. Every few minutes he emptied a pan, shook his head and began again. Beside him, a second pan lay waiting, half full of gravel, like a hungry mouth.

By noon he had found only a few grains, hardly enough to buy a bag of rice. Yet he did not complain. He explained that he had put four children through school with such grains, and that a single good day could change a family's fortune. "That is why I never stop," he said. "Hope is the real gold of this place." Behind his calm words, however, I could sense the danger of his trade: the pits that collapse after heavy rain, the mercury that poisons the water, and the cheating buyers who pay a quarter of the price.

Just as I was about to leave, his hand stopped. He lifted a tiny shining pebble between two fingers and held it up to the light. For a moment neither of us spoke. It was not a fortune, but it was enough to pay a term's fees for his youngest daughter. He closed his fist over it, smiled and whispered, "Today, the earth has been kind."

That evening, as we walked home, I thought deeply about what I had seen. The picture of a man crouching in the dust symbolises more than poverty: it represents courage, perseverance and quiet dignity. Pa Nkwain's story taught me that those who work with their hands, often scorned in our society, sustain families and communities. It also showed me that such workers deserve safer tools, fair prices and protection by the law. Above all, it taught me that success is rarely sudden; it is the reward of patient effort repeated daily, like the swirling of a pan, until the shining reward appears.

**Marking grid (20 marks)**

| Criterion | Marks | What earns the marks |
|---|---|---|
| Content and Organisation | 6 | Relevant ideas that answer the topic, developed with examples, in clear paragraphs with an introduction and a conclusion |
| Expression | 8 | Varied vocabulary and sentence structures, appropriate style and tone, fluent links between ideas |
| Accuracy | 6 | Correct grammar, tenses, spelling and punctuation |

**Common mistakes**

1. Not saying which picture is used, or describing the picture line by line with no composition built from it.
2. Writing a composition that has no clear connection with the picture, which the instruction forbids.
